mainTopic: Stories about embarrassing רב פפא; rain for an individual; signs of rain; עולא in בבל; and the dispute between רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע over where rain comes from.
overview: This amud first finishes the story of the רבנן who embarrassed רב פפא: a dream verse hinted at their punishment, and his farewell hinted at a final parting. A similar story follows: רב שימי בר אשי stopped challenging רב פפא once he heard how much it pained him. The גמרא then returns to rain. ריש לקיש proves from a פסוק in זכריה that rain can fall for one person, and a ברייתא narrows this to one field and even one plant. The story of רב דניאל בר קטינא's garden shows this happening. Next come signs of rain, פורחות clouds and drizzle, and עולא's stories in בבל about failed rain signs and painful cheap dates. Finally a ברייתא records the dispute between רבי אליעזר (rain comes from the ocean) and רבי יהושע (rain comes from the upper waters). The גמרא then matches פסוקים to each view, and the last one continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A dream verse and a farewell that hints at a final parting
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא hears a verse in a dream about cutting off three shepherds. The next day he parts from the רבנן who embarrassed him with the words 'go בשלום.'
steps.simpleTranslation: In a dream, a verse was read to him: 'And I cut off the three shepherds.' The next day, as they were leaving him, he said to them: 'Let the רבנן go in peace (בשלום).'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the story from the previous section. רב פפא gets a dream-message that the רבנן who embarrassed him will be punished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse about 'three shepherds' being cut off pointed to these three רבנן. His farewell 'go בשלום' (rather than the usual לשלום) is understood as a hint that he would not see them again. The story shows how serious it is to embarrass a תלמיד חכם.

keyTerms.meaning: They read to him (a verse was shown/read to him)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Go בשלום' sounds like an ordinary friendly goodbye. In context, though, it hints at a final parting. Elsewhere (ברכות סד.) the גמרא says בשלום is the wording used when parting from the dead.

phrases.english: They read to him in his dream:
"And I cut off the three shepherds."
The next day, when they were taking leave of him,
he said to them: Let the Rabbis go in peace.
phrases.notes: A hint that this was a final parting

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Concludes the story of רב פפא's fast, which began earlier.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Those who embarrassed רב פפא were hinted to face punishment; his farewell signaled a final parting.

steps.title: A student's constant challenges cause his teacher pain
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי בר אשי kept raising many objections against רב פפא. One day he overheard רב פפא pray to be saved from the embarrassment those questions caused.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי בר אשי was often in front of רב פפא and challenged him a lot. One day he saw him fall on his face in prayer. He heard him say: 'May the Merciful One save us from the embarrassment of שימי.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second, similar story about embarrassment. This step sets up the situation; the student's reaction comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב שימי's questions were not meant to hurt, but they still embarrassed רב פפא. רב פפא turned to ה׳ privately in נפילת אפים (the prayer said while leaning on one's arm) and asked to be spared.

keyTerms.meaning: Was often found before him (studied with him regularly)
Fell on his face (נפילת אפים, a prayer of supplication)

phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
was often found before Rav Pappa,
he would raise many objections against him.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד חַזְיֵיהּ דִּנְפַל עַל אַפֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: One day he saw him fall on his face (in prayer),
he heard him say:
May the Merciful One save us from the embarrassment of Shimi.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי הֲוָה שְׁכִיחַ קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב פָּפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel story on the same theme: the pain of embarrassing רב פפא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even well-meant challenges can cause a teacher real embarrassment.

steps.title: The student decides to stay silent
steps.stepSummary: After hearing the prayer, רב שימי בר אשי accepts silence on himself and stops challenging רב פפא.
steps.simpleTranslation: He took silence upon himself and did not challenge him anymore.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the student changing his behavior. He chose his teacher's dignity over his own questions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once רב שימי understood how much pain he was causing, he accepted silence on himself. This closes the section of stories about embarrassing רב פפא.
steps.whatToRemember: Both stories teach the same lesson: be very careful about embarrassing a תלמיד חכם, even unintentionally.

phrases.english: He accepted silence upon himself,
and no longer raised objections against him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The student's response to the prayer he overheard.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב שימי בר אשי stopped challenging רב פפא so as not to embarrass him.

steps.title: ריש לקיש also holds that rain can fall for one person
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the rain discussion. It says that ריש לקיש also holds that rain can come for the sake of a single individual (יחיד), and introduces his question about the source.
steps.simpleTranslation: And ריש לקיש also holds that rain comes for the sake of an individual. For ריש לקיש said: From where do we know that rain can come for an individual?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the stories and goes back to the topic of rain. It is setting up ריש לקיש's proof, which comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'also' (ואף) shows that ריש לקיש agrees with an opinion stated earlier in the סוגיא. Rain does not only come for a whole community; it can come for one person's needs.

keyTerms.meaning: And also (agreeing with an earlier view)
For the sake of an individual

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish also holds
rain for the sake of an individual,
as Reish Lakish said:
From where is it derived that rain falls for an individual?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ סָבַר מָטָר בִּשְׁבִיל יָחִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the aggadic stories and returns to the earlier discussion about rain for an individual.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to ריש לקיש, rain can fall for the sake of a single individual.

steps.title: The פסוק in זכריה as the source
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש brings a פסוק from זכריה. It ends with 'to each man, grass in the field.'
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'Ask ה׳ for rain at the time of the late rain; ה׳ makes thunderclouds, and He will give them showers of rain, to each man grass in the field.'
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש quotes the פסוק that proves his point. The key words are at the end: 'to a man… grass… field.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have just said that ה׳ gives rain. Instead it adds 'to a man' (לאיש), which points to a single person's needs. The next steps explain how each word is learned.

phrases.english: As it is written:
"Ask of the Lord rain at the time of the late rain;
the Lord makes thunderclouds,
and He will give them showers of rain,
to each man grass in the field."

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: שַׁאֲלוּ מֵה׳ מָטָר בְּעֵת מַלְקוֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the מנין question with a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: Rain can fall for an individual.

steps.title: The word 'to a man' shows rain for one person
steps.stepSummary: One might have thought rain comes only for everyone together. The word לאיש teaches that it can come for one person.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think rain comes only for everyone. That is why the פסוק says 'to a man.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains which word in the פסוק proves ריש לקיש's point. It uses the standard 'one might think… the verse says' method.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the word לאיש, we would assume rain is only given to the whole community. The singular word 'man' teaches that rain can be given for an individual's sake.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse teaches / therefore the verse says

phrases.english: One might think it is for everyone —
therefore the verse says: "to a man."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pinpoints the word in the פסוק that proves the rule.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word לאיש in the פסוק.

steps.title: A ברייתא narrows it further: one field, even one plant
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא narrows the פסוק in two more steps. 'Field' teaches that rain can come for only one of his fields, and 'grass' teaches that it can come for only one plant in that field.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a ברייתא teaches: If 'to a man,' you might think it is for all his fields. So the פסוק says 'field.' If 'field,' you might think it is for the whole field. So the פסוק says 'grass.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that uses the same pattern to narrow the rain down even further. It goes from a person, to one field, to a single plant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word in the פסוק adds a new level of precision. 'שדה' (singular) limits it to one field rather than all his fields. 'עשב' limits it to one plant rather than the whole field. The point is that ה׳ can send rain for even the smallest, most specific need.

keyTerms.meaning: And it was taught in a ברייתא

steps.whatToRemember: ריש לקיש holds that rain can fall for one individual (from לאיש). The ברייתא narrows it to one field (שדה) and even one plant (עשב).
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the רבנן saw rain as directly tied to ה׳'s attention to each person's specific needs, not only to the community as a whole.

phrases.english: And it was taught in a baraita:
If "to a man," one might think it is for all his fields —
therefore the verse says: "field."
If "field," one might think it is for the entire field —
therefore the verse says: "grass."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנְיָא: אִי לְאִישׁ, יָכוֹל לְכׇל שְׂדוֹתָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A ברייתא continues the derivation, narrowing the rule beyond 'an individual.'
steps.raayaObject: Rain can fall for one field and even for one plant.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The words שדה and עשב in זכריה י:א, as explained by a ברייתא.

steps.title: A garden watered only where needed
steps.stepSummary: The story of רב דניאל בר קטינא shows that rain can fall only on the specific garden beds that need water.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like רב דניאל בר קטינא, who had a garden. Every day he walked through it and said, 'This bed needs water, and that bed does not.' Then rain came and watered only the places that needed water.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a real-life story to show that the ברייתא's idea, rain for even one plant, actually happens.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 learned from the word 'grass' that rain can come for a single plant. This story shows that idea in practice. Rain fell only on the beds that רב דניאל בר קטינא said needed water and skipped the rest. The precise focus of the rain is the point of the story.
steps.whyThisMatters: It turns the ברייתא's reading of the פסוק into something that was actually seen, so the idea of 'rain for one plant' is not only theory.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּרַב דָּנִיאֵל בַּר קַטִּינָא
phrases.english: Like this case of Rav Daniel bar Ketina
he had a certain garden.

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל יוֹמָא הֲוָה אָזֵיל וְסָיַיר לַהּ.
phrases.english: Every day he would go and inspect it.
He would say: This bed needs water,
and this bed does not need water.
And rain would come and water
phrases.notes: The rain responds exactly to his words.

phrases.english: every place that needed water.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּרַב דָּנִיאֵל בַּר קַטִּינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the ברייתא's teaching that rain can come for one plant.
steps.raayaObject: Rain can be aimed at individual plants.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of רב דניאל בר קטינא's garden.

steps.title: What does 'ה׳ עושה חזיזים' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the phrase 'ה׳ עושה חזיזים' in the פסוק from זכריה means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the meaning of 'ה׳ makes חזיזים'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the פסוק of זכריה from step 5 and asks about another phrase in it. This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the סוגיא has only looked at the end of the פסוק ('לאיש עשב בשדה'). Now it asks about the earlier words. The answer will show that this phrase also fits the theme of rain for individuals.

keyTerms.meaning: rain clouds (the word is defined later)

phrases.english: What is the meaning of 'The Lord makes thunderclouds'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the פסוק in זכריה to explain another phrase in it.

steps.title: A separate cloud for each צדיק
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא explains that הקב"ה makes a separate rain cloud for every צדיק.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: This teaches that for every צדיק, הקב"ה makes a cloud just for him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא answers the question. The plural word 'חזיזים' means that there are many clouds, one for each צדיק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plural form is read as many separate clouds, not one shared cloud. This matches the theme from steps 6 and 7 that rain can come for a single person.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina said:
This teaches that for every righteous person
the Holy One, Blessed be He, makes for him
a cloud of his own.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא מְלַמֵּד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The plural 'חזיזים' means a separate cloud for each צדיק.

steps.title: חזיזים are פורחות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the word חזיזים actually refers to, and רב יהודה says it means פורחות.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are חזיזים? רב יהודה said: פורחות (flying clouds).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks what kind of cloud the word חזיזים describes. רב יהודה answers that it means פורחות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 explained why the word is plural. This step identifies what the cloud physically is. It also brings in the term פורחות, which the next few steps will build on.

phrases.english: What are 'thunderclouds'?
Rav Yehuda said: Flying clouds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the meaning of the phrase to the definition of the word.

steps.title: פורחות are a sign of rain
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that פורחות are a sign that rain is coming.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: A sign of rain is פורחות.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן adds a practical point: when you see פורחות, rain is on its way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This connects the definition from step 11 to real weather. Now that חזיזים have been identified as פורחות, we learn that these clouds announce coming rain. This statement is what the story of עולא in step 16 will test.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
A sign of rain is flying clouds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a practical sign of rain based on the term פורחות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Seeing פורחות means rain is coming.

steps.title: What פורחות look like
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא describes פורחות as a thin cloud underneath a thick cloud.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are פורחות? רב פפא said: A thin cloud under a thick cloud.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a clear description of פורחות, and רב פפא explains what they look like.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now פורחות was only a name. רב פפא gives a picture you can actually recognize: a thin cloud floating beneath a thick one. With this description, a person can use רבי יוחנן's sign.

phrases.english: What are flying clouds?
Rav Pappa said:
A thin cloud
under a thick cloud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the term used in steps 11 and 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A thin cloud under a thick cloud.

steps.title: Drizzle before and after rain
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה teaches that drizzle before rain means rain is coming, while drizzle after rain means the rain is stopping.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: Drizzle before rain means rain is coming. Drizzle after rain means the rain is stopping.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה gives a second sign of rain: light drizzle, called נהילא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same drizzle means opposite things depending on when it falls. Before rain, it announces that rain is about to come. After rain, it shows that the rain is ending.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
Drizzle before rain means rain is coming.
After rain, it means the rain is stopping.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה נְהִילָא מִקַּמֵּי מִיטְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second weather sign next to פורחות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Drizzle before rain signals rain. Drizzle after rain signals the end of the rain.

steps.title: Memory aids for the drizzle signs
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה repeats both halves of his rule and attaches a memory aid to each: a sieve and goat droppings.
steps.simpleTranslation: Before rain, rain is coming, and your sign is a sieve. After rain, the rain is stopping, and your sign is goat droppings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the two halves of רב יהודה's rule, this time to attach a memory aid (סימן) to each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sieve lets a little flour drop out before the real sifting begins, just as drizzle comes before the full rain. Goat droppings start large and end small, just as rain ends with light drizzle. The rule itself is the same as in step 14; only the memory aids are new.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new rule. It is the same rule as step 14, repeated so that each half can be given a memory aid.

phrases.english: Before rain, rain is coming.
And your memory aid is a sieve.
phrases.notes: A little flour falls out before the sifting begins.

phrases.english: That after rain, the rain is stopping.
And your memory aid is goat droppings.
phrases.notes: They start large and end small.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restates step 14 with memory aids.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sieve: drizzle before rain. Goat droppings: drizzle at the end of rain.

steps.title: עולא's failed rain forecast in בבל
steps.stepSummary: עולא saw פורחות in בבל and announced that rain was coming, but no rain fell. He joked that Babylonian rains lie just like Babylonians do.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא came to בבל and saw פורחות. He told the people, 'Put away your vessels, because rain is coming now.' In the end, no rain came. He said: 'Just as Babylonians lie, their rains lie too.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story showing that רבי יוחנן's sign of פורחות did not work in בבל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא came from ארץ ישראל and used the sign he knew from there. In בבל the sign failed. The story teaches that the sign of פורחות is reliable in ארץ ישראל but not in בבל.
steps.whatToRemember: פורחות and drizzle are signs of rain. However, the sign of פורחות proved unreliable in בבל, as עולא found out.
steps.whyThisMatters: It limits רבי יוחנן's general sign of rain to a specific place.

phrases.english: Ulla happened to come to Babylonia.
He saw flying clouds.
He said to them: Put away your vessels,
because rain is coming now.
In the end, the rain did not come.
He said: Just as Babylonians lie,
so too their rains lie.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests רבי יוחנן's sign of פורחות in בבל, where it fails.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sign of פורחות did not hold in בבל.

steps.title: עולא sees cheap dates in בבל
steps.stepSummary: עולא sees a whole basket of sweet dates sold for one זוז and wonders why the Babylonians don't learn more תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא came to בבל and saw a basket full of dates being sold for one זוז. He said: 'A basket full of honey-sweet dates for one זוז, and the Babylonians still don't busy themselves with תורה?'
steps.whatsHappening: This is a new short story about עולא, continuing the theme of his visits to בבל from the last step. He sees food that is very cheap and complains that the Babylonians should have plenty of free time to learn.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא's reasoning is that when food is this cheap, people don't need to work hard to eat. So they should have no excuse for not learning תורה full-time. The story sets up a twist that comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: a זוז, a small silver coin
honey; here it means sweet, honey-like dates

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read דּוּבְשָׁא as real bee honey. עולא is still talking about the dates. He calls them 'honey' because they are so sweet.

phrases.english: Ulla happened to come to Babylonia,
he saw a basket full of dates for one zuz.
He said: A basket full of honey (sweet dates) for one zuz,
phrases.notes: 'Honey' is a nickname for the very sweet dates.

phrases.english: and the Babylonians do not busy themselves with Torah?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second עולא-in-בבל anecdote, following his remark about Babylonian rain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עולא thinks cheap food in בבל should free the Babylonians to learn תורה, so they have no excuse.

steps.title: עולא takes back his complaint after the dates make him sick
steps.stepSummary: After eating the dates, עולא suffers at night. He reverses himself: the dates are like knives, and it is amazing the Babylonians learn at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: That night the dates caused him pain. He said: 'A basket full of knives for one זוז, and still the Babylonians busy themselves with תורה!'
steps.whatsHappening: עולא takes back what he said in the last step. Now that he has felt how much the dates hurt, he praises the Babylonians instead of criticizing them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same food that looked like a blessing turns out to be a hardship. The cheap dates are now 'knives,' so the Babylonians who learn despite that pain deserve credit. The question mark of step 17 turns into an exclamation of admiration.
steps.whatToRemember: עולא first criticized the Babylonians and then praised them. Something that looks like an easy life can actually hold hidden hardship.

phrases.english: At night they (the dates) caused him pain,
he said: A basket full of knives for one zuz,
and yet the Babylonians busy themselves with Torah!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reverses עולא's own earlier criticism.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: עולא's own earlier complaint against the Babylonians
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The cheap dates are not a pure blessing. They cause pain, so the Babylonians are actually praiseworthy.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר: the world drinks from ocean water
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי אליעזר: rain comes from ocean water that rises up from the earth, based on the פסוק 'ואד יעלה מן הארץ'.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: רבי אליעזר says the whole world drinks from the waters of the ocean, as it says: 'And a mist rose up from the earth and watered the whole face of the ground.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: where does rain come from? It brings a ברייתא where רבי אליעזר says rain comes from the ocean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר reads the פסוק literally: the water that waters the ground first goes up 'from the earth.' So the source of rain is water below, meaning the ocean, which rises up and comes back down.

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Eliezer says:
The entire world
drinks from the waters of the ocean,
as it is stated: "And a mist went up from the earth
and watered the whole face of the ground."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New topic, the source of rain, which connects to the daf's broader rain theme.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain comes from ocean water rising up, based on 'ואד יעלה מן הארץ'.

steps.title: רבי יהושע objects: ocean water is salty
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע challenges רבי אליעזר: ocean water is salty, but rain is sweet.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע said to him: 'But ocean water is salty!'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע attacks רבי אליעזר's idea with a simple fact. Rain water is fresh, so how can it come from the salty sea?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is based on what anyone can observe. If rain were just ocean water, it should taste salty. Since it doesn't, רבי אליעזר's source seems wrong.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua said to him:
But the waters of the ocean are salty!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אליעזר's position.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אליעזר's claim that rain comes from the ocean
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Ocean water is salty while rain is sweet, so rain can't come from the ocean.

steps.title: The water becomes sweet in the clouds
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר answers that the salty water becomes sweet inside the clouds.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'The waters become sweet in the clouds.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר defends his view. Yes, the water starts out salty, but it changes before it falls.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר doesn't change his source. He adds a step in between: the clouds sweeten the water. That explains why rain tastes fresh even though it comes from the ocean.

phrases.english: He said to him: They become sweet in the clouds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יהושע's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adds a process (sweetening in the clouds) that removes the contradiction
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Rain should taste salty if it comes from the ocean.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clouds sweeten the ocean water before it falls as rain.

steps.title: רבי יהושע: the world drinks from the upper waters
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע holds that rain comes from the waters above in heaven, based on 'למטר השמים תשתה מים'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע says the whole world drinks from the upper waters, as it says: 'From the rain of heaven it drinks water.'
steps.whatsHappening: Now the ברייתא gives רבי יהושע's own opinion. Rain comes from waters stored above, not from the ocean below.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע uses a different פסוק that says the land drinks 'from the rain of heaven.' For him the source is heavenly water, so the salt problem never comes up.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua says:
The entire world
drinks from the upper waters,
as it is stated: "From the rain of heaven it drinks water,"

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אוֹמֵר: כׇּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ מִמַּיִם הָעֶלְיוֹנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to רבי אליעזר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Rain comes from the upper waters, based on 'למטר השמים תשתה מים'.

steps.title: What does רבי יהושע do with the verse about mist rising?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks how רבי יהושע explains רבי אליעזר's פסוק, 'ואד יעלה מן הארץ'.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then how do I explain the פסוק 'And a mist went up from the earth'?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a challenge to רבי יהושע. The פסוק seems to say water rises from the earth, which sounds like רבי אליעזר's view. This line sets up רבי יהושע's explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every פסוק has to mean something. If רבי יהושע says rain comes from above, he must still give a meaning to the פסוק about mist going up from below.

keyTerms.meaning: how do I fulfill (explain) this פסוק?

phrases.english: But how do I uphold (explain)
"And a mist went up from the earth"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יהושע from the פסוק that רבי אליעזר used.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע's claim that rain comes from the upper waters
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק says mist rises from the earth to water the ground, which suggests the source is below.

steps.title: Clouds rise up and catch rain water from above
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע explains: the 'mist' means clouds that rise to the sky, open like a flask, and take in rain water from above.
steps.simpleTranslation: This teaches that the clouds grow strong and rise up to the sky, open their mouths like a leather flask, and receive rain water, as it says: 'They distill rain from His mist.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע answers the challenge. The thing rising from the earth is the cloud itself, not the water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The clouds rise up empty. Up above, they fill with heavenly water. So 'ואד יעלה' describes the clouds going up, and the water still comes from above. A second פסוק from איוב backs up this picture.

phrases.english: It teaches that the clouds grow strong
and rise up to the firmament,
and open their mouths like a leather flask,
and receive the rain water,
as it is stated: "They distill rain from His mist."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by reinterpreting the פסוק.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'ואד יעלה מן הארץ' means the rain water itself rises from below.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means the clouds rise up and then collect the rain water from above.

steps.title: Clouds are full of holes like a sieve
steps.stepSummary: The clouds have holes like a sieve and sprinkle the water down onto the ground, based on 'חשרת מים עבי שחקים'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the clouds are full of holes like a sieve, and they come and sprinkle water onto the ground, as it says: 'A sprinkling of water, thick clouds of the skies.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues its picture of how rain works. After the clouds fill up with water, they let it out slowly through many small holes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains how the water comes down. It does not fall in one big stream. It sprinkles down drop by drop, like through a sieve. The word חשרת in the פסוק is read as 'sprinkling.'

keyTerms.meaning: sprinkle / let out drop by drop

phrases.english: And they are perforated like a sieve,
and they come and sprinkle water
onto the ground,
as it is stated: "A sprinkling of water, thick clouds of the skies."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the description of the clouds, from collecting water to releasing it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Clouds release rain through tiny holes like a sieve, based on 'חשרת מים'.

steps.title: A day of rain is as great as the day of creation
steps.stepSummary: Only a hair's width separates one raindrop from the next, yet each falls separately. This shows that a day of rain is as great as the day heaven and earth were created.
steps.simpleTranslation: And between one drop and the next there is only the width of a hair. This teaches you that a day of rain is as great as the day heaven and earth were created.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes with a lesson. The drops fall so close together yet never merge, which is a wonder from הקב"ה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Drops only a hair apart should run together into a stream, but they don't. That shows rain is a constant miracle. So the ברייתא compares a rainy day to the day of creation.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי אליעזר says rain comes from the ocean and is sweetened in the clouds. רבי יהושע says it comes from the upper waters, and the clouds rise to collect it. Either way, rain falling drop by drop is as great a wonder as creation.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the whole מסכת treats rain so seriously. Rain is not just weather. It is a miracle on the level of creation.

phrases.english: And there is nothing between one drop and another
except the width of a hair,
to teach you that the day of rains is as great
as the day on which heaven and earth were created.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a lesson from the sieve-like way the clouds release rain.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Rainfall, with each drop falling separately, is a miracle as great as the creation of heaven and earth.

steps.title: Proof that rain is as great as creation
steps.stepSummary: Two verses about God's wonders both use the phrase 'אין חקר'. One is linked to rain and the other to creation, so rain is compared to creation.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'Who does great things past finding out,' and it is written next: 'Who gives rain upon the earth.' And it is written elsewhere: 'Have you not known, have you not heard, the everlasting God, ה׳, His understanding is past finding out' (said about creating the world). And it is written: 'Who sets the mountains firm with His strength,' etc.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the verses that prove the last statement: a day of rain is as great as the day heaven and earth were created.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'אין חקר' appear in a verse connected to rain. The same words appear in ישעיהו, in a verse about God as Creator. The shared words link the two topics, so rain is as wondrous as creation. The last verse, from a psalm about rain, also describes God's creating power.

keyTerms.meaning: Beyond searching out; too great to fully understand
As it is said; introduces a proof verse

steps.whatToRemember: The same phrase 'אין חקר' is used for both rain and creation. That shared phrase is why the day of rain is compared to the day of creation.

phrases.english: As it is said: 'Who does great things past finding out,'
and it is written: 'Who gives rain upon the earth,'
phrases.notes: This verse links the 'great things' to rain.

phrases.english: and it is written elsewhere:
'Have you not known, have you not heard,
the everlasting God, ה׳,
phrases.notes: The verse goes on to describe Him as Creator of the ends of the earth.

phrases.english: His understanding is past finding out,'
and it is written: 'Who sets the mountains firm with His strength,' etc.
phrases.notes: This comes from a psalm about rain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the verses behind step 26's claim that a day of rain equals the day of creation.
steps.raayaObject: A day of rain is as great as the day heaven and earth were created.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The phrase 'אין חקר' appears in איוב (linked to rain) and in ישעיהו (about creation).

steps.title: Whose view fits 'He waters the mountains from His upper chambers'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which opinion matches רבי יוחנן's reading that rain comes from God's upper chambers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose opinion follows this verse: 'He waters the mountains from His upper chambers'? And רבי יוחנן said: from the upper chambers of the Holy One, Blessed be He.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. It wants to know which side of the רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע argument fits this verse and רבי יוחנן's reading of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן reads 'His upper chambers' literally, as God's chambers in heaven. That suggests rain comes from above. The גמרא is setting up a match with one of the two opinions.

phrases.english: Whose opinion does this follow, which is written:
'He waters the mountains from His upper chambers,'
and Rabbi Yochanan said:
from the upper chambers of the Holy One, Blessed be He,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the רבי אליעזר / רבי יהושע dispute about where rain comes from (steps 19–24) by testing which opinion a פסוק and רבי יוחנן's reading of it follow.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which opinion, רבי אליעזר's or רבי יהושע's, fits רבי יוחנן's reading of 'מעליותיו'?

steps.title: It fits רבי יהושע
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן's reading fits רבי יהושע, who says rain comes from the waters above.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose opinion? רבי יהושע's.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי יוחנן's reading matches רבי יהושע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע holds that rain comes from the upper waters in heaven (step 22). Rain coming 'from God's upper chambers' says the same thing.

phrases.english: Whose? Like Rabbi Yehoshua.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 28.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The reading follows רבי יהושע, since he holds that rain comes from above.

steps.title: How does רבי אליעזר explain this verse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבי אליעזר would explain a verse that seems to say rain comes from heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אליעזר, how does he explain it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אליעזר. He says rain comes from the ocean below, so how does he explain 'from His upper chambers'?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse seems to support only רבי יהושע. The short words 'ורבי אליעזר' mean: what does the other opinion do with this verse? The answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: And רבי אליעזר? (meaning: how does he explain it?)

steps.confusionAlert: These two words are a full question. The גמרא often asks 'how does the other opinion explain this?' just by naming that opinion.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Eliezer (how does he explain the verse)?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to the other opinion, which the verse seems to go against.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אליעזר's view that rain comes from the ocean below
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse says rain comes 'from His upper chambers', which seems to mean from heaven, against רבי אליעזר.

steps.title: The clouds go up there, so rain is called 'from His upper chambers'
steps.stepSummary: For רבי אליעזר, the clouds rise up toward heaven, so the verse describes their rain as coming from above.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the clouds go up there, the verse calls the rain 'He waters from His upper chambers'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבי אליעזר. The verse is describing where the clouds are, not where the water came from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי אליעזר the water starts in the ocean. But the clouds holding it rise up to the sky. So the verse can say 'from His upper chambers' even though the water came from below.

keyTerms.meaning: It calls them; it describes them as

phrases.english: Since they (the clouds) go up there,
it calls them 'He waters from His upper chambers.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against רבי אליעזר.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'From His upper chambers' means the water itself starts in heaven.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse describes where the clouds are, up in the sky, not where the water started.

steps.title: Proof from 'dust from the heavens'
steps.stepSummary: The תורה says 'dust from the heavens', yet dust does not start in heaven. Something that rises up to the sky can be called 'from heaven'.
steps.simpleTranslation: For if you do not say this, how could 'powder and dust from the heavens' happen? Rather, since the dust is lifted up there, the verse calls it 'from the heavens'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the answer with another verse that clearly cannot be read literally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no dust in heaven. The verse calls it 'from the heavens' only because the wind lifts it up into the sky. The same way of speaking explains 'from His upper chambers'.

keyTerms.meaning: For if you do not say so

phrases.english: For if you do not say so,
'powder and dust from the heavens,'
how could you find such a thing?
phrases.notes: There is no dust in heaven.

phrases.english: Rather, since it is lifted up there,
it calls it 'from the heavens.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports step 31 with a parallel verse.
steps.raayaObject: Something that rises to the sky can be described as coming 'from heaven'.

steps.title: The same applies to 'from His upper chambers'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא applies the dust example to the clouds and closes the defense of רבי אליעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too here: since the clouds go up there, the verse calls them 'from His upper chambers'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up by applying the dust example back to the rain verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dust rises and is called 'from the heavens'. Clouds rise and are called 'from His upper chambers'. So the verse does not disprove רבי אליעזר.

keyTerms.meaning: So too; the same applies here

phrases.english: So too here:
since they go up there, it calls it 'from His upper chambers.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the proof of step 32 back to the verse.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both opinions can explain 'משקה הרים מעליותיו'. רבי יהושע reads it literally. רבי אליעזר reads it as describing clouds that rise to the sky.

steps.title: Whose view fits רבי חנינא's teaching about the deep waters?
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא says the deep waters filled the storehouses with grain. The גמרא asks whose view that follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose opinion follows what רבי חנינא said about 'He gathers the waters of the sea like a heap, He puts the deep waters in storehouses': What caused the storehouses to fill with grain? The deep waters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a second 'whose opinion' question. This time it is about a teaching that links crops to the deep waters below.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא reads the verse to mean that the water of the deep is what grows the grain. That points to water from below. The גמרא is setting up a match with one of the opinions.

phrases.aramaic: כְּמַאן אָזְלָא הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא:
phrases.english: Whose opinion follows what Rabbi Chanina said:
'He gathers the waters of the sea like a heap,
He puts the deep waters in storehouses.'
What caused the storehouses to be filled with grain?
The deep waters.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּמַאן אָזְלָא הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same kind of question as step 28, now about a different teaching.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which opinion fits רבי חנינא's teaching that the deep waters fill the storehouses with grain?

steps.title: It fits רבי אליעזר
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא's teaching fits רבי אליעזר, who holds that rain comes from the ocean below.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like רבי אליעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי חנינא follows רבי אליעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the deep waters grow the crops, the water comes from below. That is רבי אליעזר's view.

phrases.english: Like Rabbi Eliezer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 34.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The teaching follows רבי אליעזר, since he holds that rain comes from the waters below.

steps.title: How does רבי יהושע explain this verse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to explain how רבי יהושע would read the verse about the deep waters. The answer continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהושע? That verse...
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא asks how רבי יהושע handles this verse and starts his answer with 'that verse', which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This mirrors step 30, but now the other side must explain a verse that seems to favor רבי אליעזר. The word 'ההוא' signals that רבי יהושע will say the verse is about a different event.

keyTerms.meaning: That one (that verse); begins a re-reading

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehoshua (how does he explain it)?
That verse...
phrases.notes: The answer continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to the other opinion, the same move as step 30.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע's view that rain comes from above
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי חנינא's verse seems to show that the deep waters below feed the crops, which goes against רבי יהושע.
